§3.7 Quantization and Fock

3.7 Quantization and Fock

3.8 Scalar Field Theory

  • Scalar Field Theory is fairly similar to Classical Field Theory with the exception that it is quantized via the methods that will be presented shortly. This ensures that it obeys the laws of quantum mechanics, while still being a “Toy Theory” due to the simplicity of the objects involved in it ((potentially) complex fields 𝜙 as opposed to vectors 𝐴𝜇 or spinors 𝜓 which are closer to real, physical particles).

3.8.1 Quantization

  • As seen in ‘s Quantum Field Theory Notes, one could try to naively try to quantize the Schrodinger Equation (via the use of a series to have the equation be on-shell), which would bring rise to some problems
𝐻|𝜓⟩=𝑖𝜕𝑡|𝜓⟩𝐻=𝑝̂2+𝑚2
3.8.1.1 Harmonic Oscillator/First Quantization

  • The standard Hamiltonian for a simple harmonic oscillator is

    𝐻=12𝑝22𝑚+12𝑚𝜔2𝑥2
    . The relevance to quantization will become apparent.

Definition 3.8.1.1.1 (First Quantization).

The idea behind first quantization is to apply the commutation relation [𝑥̂,𝑝̂]=𝑖 to a system. This commutation relation is known as the canonical commutation relation, and it can be used to obtain quantum mechanics from a classical theory (which we are doing now).

  • Utilizing a change of variables to 𝑎 and 𝑎†, one can derive an alternative form for the Hamiltonian

    𝑎≡𝑚𝜔2(𝑥+𝑖𝑝𝑚𝜔), 𝑎†≡𝑚𝜔2(𝑥−𝑖𝑝𝑚𝜔)
    • 𝐻=𝜔(𝑎†𝑎+12)
      is written in a very suggestive form. Such 𝑎† and 𝑎 can be thought of as “exciting” the harmonic oscillator, as you may know from quantum mechanics.
    • The eigenstates of this Hamiltonian are eigenstates of 𝑁̂≡𝑎†𝑎
  • Notice that this hamiltonian’s eigenvalues (the energies of the eigenstates) are discrete. This is a result from quantum mechanics (or, rather, defining quantum mechanics). Such a result is the reason behind both the name Quantum Mechanics and the idea of First Quantization.

  • 𝑁̂ operator:

    • 𝑁̂|𝑛⟩=𝑛|𝑛⟩
    • 𝑎†|𝑛⟩=𝑛+1|𝑛+1⟩
    • 𝑎|𝑛⟩=𝑛|𝑛−1⟩
3.8.1.2 Heisenberg Picture
  • 𝑖dd𝑡𝑎=[𝑎,𝐻]=[𝑎,𝑎(𝑎†𝑎+12)]=𝜔(𝑎𝑎†𝑎−𝑎†𝑎𝑎)=𝜔[𝑎,𝑎†]𝑎=𝜔𝑎

  • Solution is

    𝑎(𝑡)=𝑒−𝑖𝜔𝑡𝑎(0)
3.8.1.3 Relativistic Fields

  • A common relativistic equation (heavy foreshadowing) for a (free) field is the equation

    □𝜙=0.

    • Solution to this is

      𝜙(𝑥,𝑡)=∫d3𝑝(2𝜋)3[𝑎𝑝(𝑡)𝑒𝑖𝑝⃗⋅𝑥⃗+𝑎𝑝̃(𝑡)𝑒−𝑖𝑝⃗⋅𝑥⃗]

    which is written in a fairly suggestive manner

3.8.1.4 2nd Quantization

Definition 3.8.1.4.1 (Second Quantization).

To obtain 2nd quantization (and hence quantum field theory), one can use an annihilation operator 𝑎𝑝 and a creation operator 𝑎𝑝† which exist per wave number as opposed to being universal since now, we utilize infinite harmonic oscillators which exist per 𝑝

  • Free Hamiltonian is obtained via integration over these

    𝐻=∫d3𝑝(2𝜋)3𝜔𝑝(𝑎𝑝†𝑎𝑝+12)

    with 𝜔𝑝=|𝑝⃗|

  • 2nd Quantization new things:

    • Each (of the infinitely many) point of momentum 𝑝⃗ gets its own harmonic oscillator (which we integrate over to obtain our result)
    • The 𝑛th excitation of the harmonic oscillator 𝑝⃗ as being a state with 𝑛 particles
3.8.1.5 Fock Space
  • Instead of Hilbert space ℋ︀, like in Quantum Mechanics/First Quantization, we have a Fock Space ℱ︀.

  • A Fock space ℱ︀ is the direct sum of Hilbert spaces ℋ︀𝑛, that is,

    ℱ︀=⨁𝑛ℋ︀𝑛

  • States in ℋ︀𝑛 are linear combinations of {|𝑝1𝜇…𝑝𝑛𝜇⟩}

    • Since we are using Fock Space, this means that there can be however many particles due to the direct sum over Hilbert Spaces
3.8.1.6 Momentum Notation

𝑝0=𝑝⃗2+𝑚2 so |𝑝⟩=|𝑝⃗⟩=|𝑝𝜇⟩ due to no loss of generality (this only works if it is on-shell).

3.8.1.7 Field Expansion

  • Previously, we noted that [𝑎,𝑎†]=1. This generalizes to [𝑎𝑘,𝑎𝑝†]=(2𝜋)3𝛿3(𝑝⃗−𝑘⃗)

  • 𝑎𝑝†|0⟩=12𝜔𝑝|𝑝⟩

  • ⟨0|0⟩=1 since it is the vacuum ground state

    • ⟨𝑝|𝑘⟩=2𝜔𝑝𝜔𝑘⟨0|𝑎𝑝𝑎𝑜†|0⟩=2𝜔𝑝(2𝜋)3𝛿3(𝑝⃗−𝑘⃗)

  • Identity operator

    𝟙=∫d3𝑝(2𝜋)312𝜔𝑝|𝑝⟩⟨𝑝|

  • Free field definition

    𝜙0(𝑥⃗)≡∫d3𝑝(2𝜋)312𝜔𝑝(𝑎𝑝𝑒𝑖𝑝⃗⋅𝑥⃗+𝑎𝑝†𝑒−𝑖𝑝⃗⋅𝑥⃗)

    which is why I said 𝜙(𝑥⃗,𝑡) from 4.1.2 was written in a suggestive manner (although this is still technically just a definition)

3.8.1.8 Momentum state inner product with free field
⟨𝑝⃗|𝜙0(𝑥⃗)|0⟩=⟨0|2𝜔𝑝𝑎𝑝∫d3𝑘(2𝜋)3(𝑎𝑘𝑒𝑖𝑘⃗𝑥⃗+𝑎𝑘†𝑒−𝑖𝑘⃗⋅𝑥⃗)|0⟩=∫d3𝑘(2𝜋)3𝜔𝑝𝜔𝑘[𝑒𝑖𝑘⃗⋅𝑥⃗⟨0|𝑎𝑝𝑎𝑘|0⟩+𝑒−𝑖𝑘⃗⋅𝑥⃗⟨0|𝑎𝑝𝑎𝑘†|0⟩=𝑒−𝑖𝑝⃗⋅𝑥⃗]=𝑒−𝑖𝑝⃗⋅𝑥⃗

This is the expected result of ⟨𝑝⃗|𝑥⃗⟩, and so we conclude 𝜙0(𝑥⃗)|0⟩=|𝑥⃗⟩

3.8.1.9 Time Dependence

  • Because of Heisenberg’s equations of motion, in the Heisenberg perspective, 𝑎𝑝(𝑡) and 𝑎𝑝†(𝑡) are time dependent

    • 𝑎𝑝(𝑡)=𝑒−𝑖𝜔𝑝𝑡𝑎𝑝,𝑎𝑝†(𝑡)=𝑒𝑖𝜔𝑝𝑡𝑎𝑝†

  • Heisenberg equations of motion

    • [𝐻0,𝜙0(𝑥⃗,𝑡)]=∫d3𝑝(2𝜋)3∫d3𝑘(2𝜋)312𝜔𝑘[𝜔𝑝(𝑎†𝑎𝑝+12),𝑎𝑘𝑒−𝑖𝑘𝑥+𝑎𝑘†𝑒𝑖𝑘𝑥]=∫d3𝑝(2𝜋)312𝜔𝑝[−𝜔𝑝𝑎𝑝𝑒−𝑖𝑝𝑥+𝜔𝑝𝑎𝑝†𝑒𝑖𝑝𝑥]=−𝑖𝜕𝑡𝜙0(𝑥⃗,𝑡)

    • Should have that, for any field 𝜙,

      [𝐻,𝜙(𝑥⃗,𝑡)]=𝑖𝜕𝑡𝜙(𝑥⃗,𝑡)
      • 𝜙(𝑥⃗,𝑡)=∫d3𝑝(2𝜋)312𝜔𝑝[𝑎𝑝(𝑡)𝑒−𝑖𝑝𝑥+𝑎𝑝†(𝑡)𝑒𝑖𝑝𝑥]
        is the solution to the Heisenberg equations of motion for 𝜙, our field which does not necessarily have to be free in this case
